what_its_for: Magnesium is a mineral your body needs to stay healthy. It helps your muscles and nerves work properly, keeps your heart rhythm steady, supports strong bones, and helps control blood sugar and blood pressure. It is used to treat or prevent low magnesium levels in the body (hypomagnesemia). It may also be used for constipation relief, leg cramps, migraines, and to support heart and kidney health.
how_to_take: Take magnesium exactly as your doctor or pharmacist tells you. Most forms are taken by mouth with a full glass of water (8 ounces). You can take it with food or milk if it upsets your stomach. Do not crush or chew extended-release tablets — swallow them whole. If you are using a powder form, mix it completely in water or juice before drinking. If you are using magnesium citrate as a laxative, drink the entire bottle and follow with extra water.
dosing: The dose depends on why you are taking magnesium and what form you are using. A typical adult dose for low magnesium is 200–400 mg per day, often taken once daily or split into two doses. For constipation, magnesium citrate is usually taken as a single dose (about 10 ounces for adults). Always follow the dose your doctor or the product label recommends. Do not take more than the recommended amount without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not double up or take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store magnesium at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it in a dry place away from moisture and heat — do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the container tightly closed and out of reach of children and pets. If using magnesium citrate liquid, refrigerate it after opening for better taste and use it promptly. Do not use after the expiration date on the package.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking magnesium within 2 hours of certain antibiotics (like tetracyclines or fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin) or bisphosphonates (like alendronate), as magnesium can reduce how well those medicines work. Avoid taking more than the recommended dose, as too much magnesium can cause diarrhea, nausea, or more serious problems. Limit alcohol while taking magnesium. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before taking other supplements or antacids that also contain magnesium, to avoid getting too much.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: severe diarrhea or stomach cramps that do not go away, muscle weakness or difficulty moving, irregular or slow heartbeat, difficulty breathing, feeling faint or very dizzy, confusion or mental changes, or signs of an allergic reaction (rash, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing). Also call if your symptoms do not improve or get worse while taking magnesium.
when_it_works: For correcting low magnesium levels, you may start to feel better within a few days, but it can take 1–2 weeks to fully restore levels in your body. As a laxative, magnesium citrate usually works within 30 minutes to 6 hours. For ongoing benefits like bone health or blood pressure support, consistent daily use over several weeks to months is needed.
special_populations: Older adults: Older people may have lower magnesium levels and may need to take it regularly, but kidney function should be checked first since magnesium is removed by the kidneys. Kidney disease: If you have kidney problems, do not take magnesium without your doctor's approval — your kidneys may not be able to remove excess magnesium, which can build up to dangerous levels. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Magnesium is generally considered safe during pregnancy and breastfeeding at recommended doses, but always check with your doctor before taking any supplement. Children: Doses for children are lower and weight-based — never give a child adult-dose magnesium without a doctor's guidance.
